title: AVA: A Video Dataset of Spatio-Temporally Localized Atomic Visual Actions
limitations: AVA is a video action-recognition benchmark and does not validate prompt wording or still-illustration quality.
Its movie-derived samples and 80-label vocabulary are not a complete or culturally neutral inventory of human action.
Several labels require short temporal context, so a single rendered frame may not support the same distinction.
Dataset frequency and benchmark difficulty do not establish aesthetic desirability or a runtime sampling prior.

title: BABEL: Bodies, Action and Behavior With English Labels
limitations: BABEL is based on motion-capture sequences and does not directly represent hands, props, clothing, facial expression, or environmental consequences at illustration detail.
Its English labels and collected motion repertoire are not a universal linguistic or cultural action ontology.
Motion capture coverage can underrepresent disabled, assisted, nonhuman, highly stylized, or physically constrained embodiments.
Observed class counts and segment durations must not be converted into aesthetic frequency weights.

research_questions: Which action units remain meaningful when character identity, genre, setting, and prop category are changed?
Which body, contact, and direction cues let one still frame support an action claim without hidden temporal context?
How can concurrent actions be combined without turning a sparse scene into an unreadable composite activity?
How should action availability expand with creativity while avoiding dataset-frequency or novelty-for-its-own-sake priors?

mechanisms.statement: Represent a scene with observable fine-scale actions instead of treating a profession, activity, or genre scenario as one indivisible label.
AVA annotates multiple co-occurring atomic action labels for one visible person, so action categories need not be mutually exclusive.
Treat body actions as bounded intervals that may overlap rather than as one permanent character attribute.
Preserve transition motion as a meaningful state between stable actions instead of forcing every pose into a completed verb.
Store action atoms outside topic routes so a compatible action can be reused with unrelated character and world concepts.
Choose one primary action and at most one compatible secondary action to preserve silhouette, hand, and target legibility.
For actions that video annotators need temporal context to distinguish, require contact, support, direction, or state-change evidence in the selected still phase.
Do not use source label counts, motion frequency, or benchmark prevalence as an automatic preference for ordinary or supposedly attractive actions.

candidate_definitions.atomic_general_actions_router: Open universal action slots after explicit subject, embodiment, and scene constraints are fixed; this router is not itself a visible action.
candidate_definitions.atomic_general_actions_pose_anchor: Show one load-bearing body state through feet, seat, knee, hand, wing, tail, mobility aid, or another declared support contacting a surface.
candidate_definitions.atomic_general_actions_directional_motio: Show a body or limb displacement toward, away from, across, around, up, or down relative to one visible target.
candidate_definitions.atomic_general_actions_object_contact: Show touch, grasp, hold, manipulate, support, or release through plausible contact points and object response.
candidate_definitions.atomic_general_actions_person_interactio: Show one action directed toward another subject through contact, exchange path, reciprocal orientation, or shared target rather than a relationship label alone.
candidate_definitions.atomic_general_actions_body_support_chan: Show weight transferring between old and new supports, with unequal loading, lifted contact, or a recovering balance line.
candidate_definitions.atomic_general_actions_concurrent_layers: Show one primary action and one compatible secondary action in distinct body or interaction channels without assigning two equal focal events.
candidate_definitions.atomic_general_actions_transition_motion: Show an incomplete change between stable actions through asymmetrical support, unfinished placement, or a still-open gap to the target.
candidate_definitions.atomic_general_actions_static_ambiguity_: Reject or weaken action wording that a single frame cannot distinguish unless contact, direction, support, or before-and-after state evidence is visible.
candidate_definitions.atomic_general_actions_frequency_prior_g: Prevent source frequency, benchmark prevalence, or familiar genre repetition from becoming the default aesthetic ranking of action candidates.
candidate_definitions.atomic_general_actions_silhouette_legibi: Measure whether the primary action remains distinguishable from subject silhouette, limb direction, and target placement at thumbnail scale.
candidate_definitions.atomic_general_actions_temporal_overlap_: Measure whether concurrent action layers remain separately traceable and physically compatible at the depicted instant.

pixel_evidence_definitions.atomic_general_actions_pose_anchor: At least one declared support visibly meets a surface and the body mass is plausibly organized over or against it.
pixel_evidence_definitions.atomic_general_actions_directional_motio: A readable limb or body vector terminates at or departs from one visible target without depending on a captioned verb.
pixel_evidence_definitions.atomic_general_actions_object_contact: Fingers, palm, limb, tool interface, or another declared effector meets the object at a plausible location and the object orientation agrees with the force.
pixel_evidence_definitions.atomic_general_actions_person_interactio: Two subjects are connected by a contact point, exchange path, reciprocal facing, or shared target that is visible in the crop.
pixel_evidence_definitions.atomic_general_actions_body_support_chan: Old and new supports carry visibly unequal loads, with a lifted heel, compressed limb, displaced center line, or comparable embodiment-specific cue.
pixel_evidence_definitions.atomic_general_actions_concurrent_layers: The primary and secondary actions occupy separable effectors or relation paths and one remains visually dominant.
pixel_evidence_definitions.atomic_general_actions_transition_motion: The frame retains an unclosed distance, unfinished placement, or unstable support configuration that rules out a fully settled state.

compatibility: A pose anchor can accompany any action when it clarifies support rather than becoming a second focal event.
Directional motion is compatible with a visible target, path, or destination and with the scene crop preserving both endpoints.
Object contact is compatible with prop affordance and with hand or effector occupancy left open by fixed user requirements.
Person interaction is compatible with ensemble blocking when each participant has a readable role and no identity constraint is overwritten.
One concurrent secondary action is compatible when it uses a different body channel and supports the same event beat.
conflicts: Two actions that require the same hand, mouth, limb, tail, or tool interface at the same instant conflict unless sequentiality is explicitly depicted.
A settled symmetrical pose conflicts with wording that claims rapid transition unless another strong motion or state cue carries it.
A no-prop request conflicts with object-contact atoms and must close that slot rather than substitute an unsolicited object.
A lone-subject request conflicts with person-interaction atoms unless the other participant is an explicitly allowed off-frame target.
Uniformly equal action salience conflicts with the primary-secondary budget.
counterexamples: A standing character can be standing while performing a more important hand action, so standing is not always the primary action.
A raised arm does not by itself distinguish waving, reaching, shielding, surrendering, or stretching.
A hand near an object does not prove grasping or using it without contact and load evidence.
Motion blur does not by itself establish direction, action identity, or temporal phase.
An unusual action can be appropriate at low creativity when the user explicitly requests it, while a familiar action can be inappropriate at high creativity when it violates fixed constraints.
boundaries: Do not infer personality, intent, consent, competence, occupation, or moral status from an observed action alone.
Do not turn dangerous actions into operational instructions or add unsafe detail merely to increase novelty.
Do not overwrite user-fixed pose, action, mobility aid, handedness, limb count, no-prop, or no-people constraints.
Do not claim an exact temporal sequence from one still frame when only a compatible pose is visible.
Treat action names as retrieval labels; final prompt evidence must remain observable and embodiment-aware.
domain_limits: The source corpora emphasize human video and motion capture, so transfer to nonhuman, mechanical, magical, microscopic, or abstract subjects is a design extension.
Atomic actions do not replace topic-specific knowledge needed for specialized sports, craft, medicine, weapons, ritual, or machinery.
Video-localization labels do not establish which instant is compositionally strongest in a still illustration.
Everyday action coverage does not imply commercial appeal, genre fit, or narrative importance.
embodiment_limits: Translate support, reach, contact, and direction through the declared anatomy instead of assuming two arms, five-fingered hands, bipedal stance, or human joints.
Mobility aids, prostheses, seated bodies, limited range of motion, and assisted actions are valid action structures rather than degraded variants.
Do not equate stillness, sitting, lying, or low-amplitude motion with passivity or incapacity.
Reject physically impossible occupancy and force paths unless the world contract explicitly supplies a supernatural or mechanical bridge.
cultural_limits: Gesture meanings, exchange etiquette, interpersonal distance, gaze expectations, and preferred handedness can vary across communities and contexts.
English action labels must not be treated as a culturally exhaustive partition of movement.
Ritual, sacred, martial, and occupational actions require context-specific research rather than generic visual substitution.
Do not rank culturally familiar actions as more natural merely because they are more common in the cited datasets.
source_biases: AVA draws from selected movie intervals and therefore reflects filmmaking, casting, annotation, and label-vocabulary biases.
BABEL inherits motion-capture participant, task, sensor, and English-description biases from its contributing data.
Both sources optimize machine-recognition coverage rather than illustration creativity, viewer affect, or authorial composition.
Neither source justifies using observed action frequencies as aesthetic priors.
runtime_implications: Run this universal action router only after fixed identity, anatomy, occupancy, no-prop, no-people, and user-specified action constraints are resolved.
Select one primary atomic action and optionally one compatible secondary layer; never fill every open action channel.
Use creativity to widen semantic distance among compatible actions, not to relax contact, anatomy, safety, or fixed-constraint guards.
Require visual evidence for any action that depends on temporal context, and downgrade to a pose-state description when evidence is insufficient.
Keep topic-route frequency and dataset frequency out of action scoring; use deterministic seed, compatibility, distance, and repetition controls instead.
evaluation_implications: Test the same action candidates on unseen human, nonhuman, mechanical, seated, mobility-aid, and no-limb concepts.
At native and thumbnail scale, have reviewers identify the primary action from pixels without seeing the prompt and record ambiguity rather than forcing agreement.
Check hand or effector occupancy, support geometry, target presence, and force direction for every selected visual atom.
Compare low, medium, and high creativity under identical fixed concepts to confirm that semantic distance changes while physical compatibility does not.
Audit selection logs to verify that source frequency is absent from ranking and that repeated familiar actions do not dominate unrelated routes.

title: The Berkeley FrameNet Project
limitations: FrameNet is a lexical-semantic resource, not a visual scene-graph or illustration dataset.
The 1998 project paper describes an English resource whose frames and lexical coverage are not culturally or linguistically exhaustive.
Frame elements are frame-specific and do not justify forcing one fixed actor-target schema onto every event.
Mapping semantic participants to pose, contact, gaze, or object-state pixels is a design inference that requires rendered-image validation.

title: The Proposition Bank: An Annotated Corpus of Semantic Roles
limitations: PropBank annotates linguistic predicates and arguments rather than visible event participants in images.
Numbered arguments are defined relative to predicate rolesets and must not be assigned one global semantic meaning across all verbs.
The source corpus is English newswire-centered and is not a universal model of CJK grammar, dialogue, visual narration, or omitted participants.
Argument frequency and annotation convenience do not establish visual salience, narrative importance, or candidate preference.

research_questions: Which participant roles are necessary to make an event visually traceable without forcing every possible role into the frame?
How can actor, action, target, instrument, recipient, path, and result remain independent of character concept and prop category?
Which visible relations support a role assignment, and when should the runtime preserve ambiguity or omit a role?
How should linguistic frame resources be abstracted without imposing English syntax or predicate-frequency bias on still illustrations?

mechanisms.statement: Represent an event as a situation with frame-specific participant roles rather than as a free list of unrelated nouns.
Keep the wording that evokes an event separate from the participant slots needed to realize that event.
Resolve core and adjunct roles relative to the selected action predicate rather than assuming that argument numbers have one global meaning.
Preserve role ambiguity when two predicates organize the same entities differently instead of treating subject and object position as universal semantics.
Select only the participants necessary to trace the intended event, leaving optional roles unfilled when they add clutter or unsupported claims.
Expose actor, action, affected target, instrument, recipient or goal, path, and result as reusable slots outside topic routes while allowing predicate-specific omissions.
Ground every selected role through contact, orientation, path, support, gaze, or state difference rather than relying on a captioned role name.
Claim a result only when the affected target or environment shows a state that differs visibly from the ongoing action setup.
Do not convert frequent arguments or common corpus realizations into automatic visual focal priority.

candidate_definitions.event_role_frames_router: Build a minimal predicate-specific event frame after user-fixed subject, action, prop, population, and composition constraints are resolved; this router is not visible content.
candidate_definitions.event_role_frames_action_predicate: Realize the selected action through one observable contact, displacement, support, or state-change relation rather than a genre activity label.
candidate_definitions.event_role_frames_actor_anchor: Place the participant that initiates, controls, experiences, or bears the selected predicate in a visually traceable relation without assuming all subjects are agents.
candidate_definitions.event_role_frames_affected_target: Show the entity whose position, condition, possession, attention, or support relation changes under the action.
candidate_definitions.event_role_frames_instrument_link: Show an optional tool or mediating object physically connecting actor and target, with a plausible grip, contact point, and force or information path.
candidate_definitions.event_role_frames_recipient_goal: Show the participant or destination toward which an object, signal, movement, or effect is directed.
candidate_definitions.event_role_frames_source_goal_path: Show a readable origin-to-destination path using spacing, orientation, trajectory residue, or ordered contact points.
candidate_definitions.event_role_frames_result_state: Show a visible changed condition of the affected target or environment that can support a completed-result claim.
candidate_definitions.event_role_frames_shared_object_handoff: Show actor, transferable object, and recipient in one connected exchange geometry with possession still legible or deliberately unresolved.
candidate_definitions.event_role_frames_role_omission_guard: Leave optional participant slots empty when the predicate does not require them, the crop cannot show them, or the user has closed the corresponding people or prop slot.
candidate_definitions.event_role_frames_role_assignment_guard: Reject role assignments based only on grammatical position, stereotype, object category, gaze direction, or assumed intent when visible relations remain ambiguous.
candidate_definitions.event_role_frames_role_traceability_metr: Measure whether each selected participant can be followed through a visible relation to the action predicate and whether any unlinked entity is falsely presented as causal.

pixel_evidence_definitions.event_role_frames_action_predicate: One contact, displacement, support, transfer, or state-change relation is visible at the event center.
pixel_evidence_definitions.event_role_frames_actor_anchor: The initiating, controlling, experiencing, or affected participant is connected to the event center by body orientation, contact, path, or state evidence.
pixel_evidence_definitions.event_role_frames_affected_target: The target occupies the endpoint of the action relation and shows displacement, deformation, changed support, changed possession, or another declared effect.
pixel_evidence_definitions.event_role_frames_instrument_link: The mediating object is held or supported plausibly and contacts, points toward, carries, or transforms the target along one continuous relation.
pixel_evidence_definitions.event_role_frames_recipient_goal: The recipient or destination is visibly located at the endpoint of a transfer, signal, movement, or effect path.
pixel_evidence_definitions.event_role_frames_source_goal_path: Origin and destination remain visible or are marked by ordered spatial, material, or trajectory cues that do not contradict the action direction.
pixel_evidence_definitions.event_role_frames_result_state: A changed target or environmental condition is visible and differs from the active setup without needing explanatory text.
pixel_evidence_definitions.event_role_frames_shared_object_handoff: Two participants are connected through one transferable object by dual contact, a narrowed handoff gap, or a clearly changing possession relation.

compatibility: Actor, action, and affected target form a compact default frame when all three are visibly traceable.
An instrument is compatible only when it mediates the selected action and the actor has a free plausible effector or support.
A recipient or goal is compatible with transfer, communication, approach, placement, and directed-effect predicates.
A result state is compatible with an aftermath or completion phase when the target change is visible.
A shared-object handoff is compatible with interpersonal tension or cooperation when the object remains the single event junction.
conflicts: An instrument that never contacts, points toward, carries, or otherwise mediates the event conflicts with the claimed instrument role.
Multiple equal targets conflict with a single-target event unless the predicate and composition explicitly support a group effect.
A completed result state conflicts with a still-unstarted action phase unless the image distinguishes a previous result from the current action.
A no-people, lone-subject, or no-prop constraint closes the corresponding actor, recipient, or instrument slot rather than inviting a substitute.
Assigning every available role conflicts with the minimal visible role set and creates semantic as well as visual clutter.
counterexamples: The grammatical subject can be an experiencer or affected participant rather than the causal actor.
A held object is not necessarily an instrument; it can be a target, cargo, gift, evidence, obstacle, or unrelated possession.
A person looking at an event is not automatically its actor, recipient, or beneficiary.
A broken object does not prove that the nearest character broke it.
An empty optional role is not missing data when the predicate, crop, or user contract does not require that participant.
boundaries: Do not infer intent, culpability, consent, ownership, benefit, relationship, or emotional state from spatial proximity alone.
Do not force actor-target language onto stative, reciprocal, ambient, collective, involuntary, or experiencer-centered events.
Do not add an instrument, recipient, or result that the user explicitly excluded or that lacks visible support.
Do not convert linguistic annotation conventions into claims about universal cognition or visual storytelling.
Keep dangerous instruments and actions subject to independent safety and operational-detail guards.
domain_limits: FrameNet and PropBank cover linguistic predicates; specialized scientific, medical, legal, ritual, tactical, and technical events require domain-specific role research.
Abstract events such as remembering, promising, belonging, or social status may not have a faithful single-frame physical role structure.
Still illustration cannot directly encode tense, duration, modality, negation, or causation without additional visible evidence.
Topic-specific lore may alter causal roles, but the runtime must still expose the visible bridge rather than relying on lore labels alone.
embodiment_limits: Actor and instrument links must use the declared anatomy, appendages, interfaces, magic system, remote control, or assistive device rather than assuming human hands.
A passive or supported participant can be central to the event without being visually subordinate or morally diminished.
Collective, distributed, swarm, vehicle, environmental, and noncorporeal actors may require several spatial anchors instead of one body center.
Do not treat atypical movement, communication, sensory access, or assistance as evidence of a different semantic role.
cultural_limits: English predicate and argument structure does not map one-to-one onto Korean, Chinese, Japanese, sign languages, or culturally specific event descriptions.
Omitted subjects, serial verbs, causatives, honorific relations, classifiers, directionals, and topic-prominent constructions can organize roles differently.
Gift exchange, ritual handling, service, authority, kinship, and collective agency require context-sensitive role interpretation.
Avoid turning culturally learned props or gestures into universal actor, recipient, status, or moral-role signals.
source_biases: FrameNet began as an English lexical resource and its documented frames reflect lexicographic coverage and annotation choices.
PropBank is grounded in an English treebank and predicate-specific rolesets, with newswire and annotation-convention biases.
Both resources privilege expressed linguistic arguments, while visual scenes may omit, merge, obscure, or ambiguously stage participants.
Neither source provides aesthetic salience weights, commercial priorities, or still-image quality evidence.
runtime_implications: Build the event frame after atomic action selection so the predicate determines which participant slots can open.
Fill actor, affected target, instrument, recipient or goal, path, and result sparsely; never require all slots for every event.
Use visible contact, orientation, path, support, and state change to score role traceability before prompt emission.
Preserve ambiguity or omit a role when evidence is insufficient; creativity may introduce a semantically distant participant only with a causal and physical bridge.
Coordinate with temporal-phase selection so result state, handoff geometry, and active contact do not contradict the chosen instant.
evaluation_implications: Test role frames across unseen concepts using the same predicate with human, nonhuman, mechanical, magical, group, and assisted embodiments.
Blind reviewers should identify the event junction and trace each selected participant from pixels without access to role labels.
Include adversarial cases where a nearby prop is not an instrument, a bystander is not an actor, and damage has no visible cause.
Check CJK-language prompts and pro-drop or causative constructions for stable visual roles without requiring English surface syntax.
Measure role precision, omitted-role correctness, event readability at thumbnail scale, and violations of fixed no-prop or population constraints separately.

title: Temporal Action Localization by Structured Maximal Sums
limitations: The work addresses video localization and models start, middle, and end for recognition; it does not prescribe a six-stage illustration grammar.
Its phase components are learned from temporal windows and cannot be recovered automatically from one still frame.
The THUMOS action benchmark emphasizes particular activities and does not establish universal phase durations or visual appeal.
Translating start, middle, and end into anticipation, contact, peak, recovery, and aftermath pixels is a design inference.

title: Temporal Action Detection With Structured Segment Networks
limitations: Structured Segment Networks optimize temporal detection and completeness in video, not selection of a still-image narrative instant.
Starting, course, and ending stages do not universally correspond to contact, force peak, release, or emotional aftermath.
The benchmark domains and proposal distributions are not a neutral sample of human or fictional action.
No source result supports using stage frequency, duration, or recognition confidence as an aesthetic sampling weight.

research_questions: Which instant from anticipation through aftermath supplies the clearest still-image evidence for a selected action?
How can phase cues remain reusable across unrelated subjects, props, genres, and embodiments without pretending all actions share identical biomechanics?
What adjacent-phase residue is sufficient to imply temporal direction while keeping one focal instant?
How can the runtime prevent video-stage frequency or duration from becoming an aesthetic prior?

mechanisms.statement: Model an action as temporally evolving start, middle, and end components rather than assuming every frame is an interchangeable example of the verb.
Use starting, course, and ending evidence jointly when judging whether an action instance is complete or fragmentary.
Expect different portions of an action interval to carry different evidence and avoid judging the whole event from a phase-neutral pose alone.

Expand video start, course, and end into an illustration-facing ladder of anticipation, onset, contact or commitment, course peak, release or recovery, and aftermath, explicitly as a design inference.
Select one focal phase and at most one adjacent-phase residue so the frame implies change without depicting incompatible instants simultaneously.
Mark anticipation with a loaded body or directed attention plus a still-open distance, unmade contact, or unchanged target state.
Mark contact or commitment with a visible effector-target junction, plausible force direction, and the first target response when applicable.
Mark aftermath with released force, changed target or environment state, displaced material, or settling posture rather than generic motion effects.
Do not turn benchmark stage prevalence, duration, localization confidence, or recognition ease into a preferred still-image phase.

candidate_definitions.action_temporal_phases_router: Choose the still-image phase only after the atomic action, event roles, embodiment, and fixed user timing have been resolved; this router is not visible content.
candidate_definitions.action_temporal_phases_pre_action_antici: Show preparation before action onset through directional attention, loaded support, readied effector, and a visibly unclosed relation to the target.
candidate_definitions.action_temporal_phases_action_onset: Show the first departure from rest or the first support, orientation, or spacing change while the full action result remains absent.
candidate_definitions.action_temporal_phases_contact_commitmen: Show the effector, instrument, or body meeting the target with a plausible force, transfer, latch, or support junction and an incipient response.
candidate_definitions.action_temporal_phases_course_peak: Show the action course at its strongest readable displacement, deformation, balance demand, exchange tension, or directional contrast.
candidate_definitions.action_temporal_phases_release_recovery: Show contact or exertion ending through separating effectors, relaxing deformation, returning balance, decelerating material, or re-established support.
candidate_definitions.action_temporal_phases_aftermath_trace: Show the changed target, disturbed environment, residue, displaced objects, or settled body state after the main force or transfer has ended.
candidate_definitions.action_temporal_phases_adjacent_phase_re: Retain one physically compatible cue from the immediately previous or next phase to imply direction without combining distant instants.
candidate_definitions.action_temporal_phases_temporal_overclai: Prevent claims about sequence, duration, completion, causation, or intention that are not supported by the selected phase and its visible traces.
candidate_definitions.action_temporal_phases_single_phase_guar: Prevent simultaneous selection of incompatible anticipation, peak, recovery, and aftermath states for the same effector-target relation.
candidate_definitions.action_temporal_phases_phase_legibility_: Measure whether blind viewers can distinguish the selected broad phase from adjacent phases using pixels rather than the prompt text.
candidate_definitions.action_temporal_phases_physical_continui: Measure whether body support, contact, target state, material motion, and adjacent-phase residue form a physically continuous local sequence.

pixel_evidence_definitions.action_temporal_phases_pre_action_antici: A readied effector or loaded body aims toward a visible target while a gap, untouched surface, or unchanged target state proves onset has not occurred.
pixel_evidence_definitions.action_temporal_phases_action_onset: Support, orientation, spacing, or local motion has begun to change, but the target lacks the full contact deformation, transfer, or result associated with later phases.
pixel_evidence_definitions.action_temporal_phases_contact_commitmen: Effector or instrument meets the target at a plausible junction and the target shows the first pressure, transfer, attachment, or support response.
pixel_evidence_definitions.action_temporal_phases_course_peak: Displacement, deformation, directional contrast, balance demand, or transfer tension is near its strongest readable state while the action relation remains active.
pixel_evidence_definitions.action_temporal_phases_release_recovery: The active junction is separating or relaxing, body mass is returning to support, and residual target or material response still points back to the action.
pixel_evidence_definitions.action_temporal_phases_aftermath_trace: Active force or transfer has ended, while changed object state, residue, debris, disturbed cloth or hair, surface trace, or a settling pose remains visible.
pixel_evidence_definitions.action_temporal_phases_adjacent_phase_re: One secondary cue belongs to the immediately neighboring phase and is physically compatible with the focal phase rather than duplicating a distant instant.

compatibility: Anticipation is compatible with clear target direction and an open gap that preserves not-yet-completed status.
Onset is compatible with subtle imbalance or support change when the result is intentionally withheld.
Contact or commitment is compatible with a visible actor-target or instrument-target junction and plausible reaction.
Course peak is compatible with diagonal composition, maximum separation, deformation, or transfer tension when anatomy and cropping remain legible.
Release or recovery and aftermath are compatible with residue, displaced material, changed target state, or returning support rather than generic blur.
One adjacent-phase residue is compatible when it clarifies temporal direction without becoming a second focal event.
conflicts: Anticipation conflicts with a fully completed target result for the same event unless that result belongs to an earlier explicitly separate action.
Contact conflicts with a visible gap between the claimed effector and target unless the world contract supplies a readable remote mechanism.
Peak exertion conflicts with fully relaxed support and settled materials when they describe the same instant.
Recovery conflicts with increasing deformation or accelerating approach unless separate actors or event layers are clearly distinguished.
Aftermath conflicts with active uncompleted transfer when both are assigned to the same object and event.
Multiple distant phases selected for one relation conflict with the single-phase guard.
counterexamples: A dramatic pose with wind-blown clothing is not necessarily anticipation because no target or uncompleted relation may be visible.
Physical contact is not always the action peak; gentle handoff, inspection, remote operation, and sustained support can peak elsewhere.
The middle of a video segment is not guaranteed to be the most informative or aesthetically useful still frame.
Motion blur can occur during onset, peak, recovery, camera movement, or stylized stillness and therefore does not identify phase alone.
Broken or displaced scenery can predate the depicted actor and does not prove that the current action caused it.
A quiet aftermath can carry more narrative information than a peak-action frame without being less creative.
boundaries: Do not claim causation, intent, consent, culpability, victory, injury, death, or chronology from residue or body position alone.
Do not add gore, tactical operation, dangerous procedure, or self-harm detail as phase evidence.
Do not override an explicit user request for a particular instant, static portrait, no-action scene, or deliberately ambiguous timing.
Do not use phase labels as emotional or personality diagnoses.
When static pixels cannot separate adjacent phases, emit the observable relation and preserve uncertainty rather than asserting a hidden sequence.
domain_limits: Cyclic, continuous, simultaneous, ambient, stochastic, ritual, conversational, and purely mental events may not fit a single linear anticipation-to-aftermath ladder.
Very fast impacts, microscopic changes, remote digital actions, magical causation, and long-duration transformations require domain-specific evidence bridges.
Video localization models do not determine the best narrative or commercial still for illustration.
An aftermath may outlast the depicted actor or action by an unknown duration, which a single image cannot recover.
embodiment_limits: Phase cues must follow the declared anatomy, supports, actuators, sensory channels, mobility aids, materials, and physics rather than a default bipedal human arc.
Nonhuman ears, tails, wings, tentacles, wheels, tracks, distributed bodies, or magical interfaces can carry preload, contact, and recovery evidence.
Limited range of motion, tremor, assistance, low-amplitude action, or atypical timing does not make a phase less valid or less legible by definition.
Do not demand exaggerated joint extension, balance risk, or strain to make an action readable.
cultural_limits: Narrative conventions for the decisive moment, restraint, aftermath, ritual sequence, and displayed exertion vary across traditions and genres.
A source benchmark stage structure must not be presented as a universal storytelling law.
Culturally specific ritual or martial phase boundaries require dedicated sources and should not be approximated from generic action footage.
Do not equate high-energy peak phases with greater value, heroism, masculinity, competence, or commercial appeal.
source_biases: Both sources optimize temporal localization on video benchmarks rather than still-image communication, creativity, or authorial composition.
Start, middle, course, and end partitions are modeling choices and do not prove one natural phase taxonomy for all actions.
Benchmark activity selection, clip duration, camera editing, and annotation boundaries can bias which phase cues appear discriminative.
Neither source supports importing stage frequency, duration, or recognition score as an aesthetic prior.
runtime_implications: Resolve fixed user timing first; if timing is open, choose one phase after atomic action and event-role compatibility are established.
Use creativity to explore less expected but causally legible phases, including quiet anticipation or aftermath, without relaxing physical continuity.
Permit at most one adjacent-phase residue and reject distant phase combinations for the same effector-target relation.
Require phase-specific pixel evidence and downgrade unsupported sequence claims to observable pose, contact, or state wording.
Coordinate aftermath with event-result state and prop-state modules, and coordinate contact with hand-object and support geometry.
Exclude source phase frequency, duration, and detector confidence from selection scoring.
evaluation_implications: For the same unseen action and concept, generate or inspect anticipation, onset, contact, peak, recovery, and aftermath variants under fixed identity and composition constraints.
Blind reviewers should classify broad phase and cite visible cues; ambiguous cases count as ambiguity rather than forced errors.
Check physical continuity across adjacent variants for support, contact, force direction, object state, garment response, and environmental residue.
Include cyclic, remote, nonhuman, assisted, no-prop, and no-action holdouts to test when the linear router should abstain or adapt.
Compare creativity levels to verify that phase surprise can increase while temporal overclaim, anatomy violations, and incompatible multi-phase selection do not.
Audit candidate logs to confirm no benchmark-frequency or duration feature influences phase ranking.
